page: Amazon Web Services m7i.metal-24xl is a bare-metal general-purpose server powered by dedicated Intel Xeon 8488C processors. Operating on the x86_64 architecture, it features 96 virtual CPUs across 48 physical cores with a base clock speed of 3.2 GHz. The processor configuration includes a 105 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for accelerated matrix operations. The system is equipped with 384.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced allocation of 4.0 GB per physical core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPUs, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 38 Gbps.

In benchmark evaluations, the m7i.metal-24xl demonstrates top-tier multi-core performance, placing in the top 10% for Geekbench multi-core, Passmark CPU, and Passmark CPU encryption tests. Its architectural enhancements yield strong results in specialized workloads, achieving top 10% rankings in ray tracing, image processing, and text processing. Memory performance is robust, with uncached large-block read bandwidth reaching 231.55 GB/sec, though the overall Passmark memory score falls in the average tier. The server also exhibits strong capabilities in database operations, static web serving at 86.24 GB/sec, and CPU-based LLM inference, processing 292.47 tokens/sec for medium-sized 7B model prompts.

As a bare-metal instance, the m7i.metal-24xl offers high resource density and eliminates virtualization overhead, making it a qualitatively cost-efficient choice for workloads requiring direct hardware access and predictable performance. However, the lack of local NVMe storage means all storage operations must traverse the network, which may introduce latency compared to storage-optimized instances. The absence of a dedicated GPU also limits its utility for heavy deep learning training, though its AMX instructions mitigate this for CPU-based inference. This server is highly suited for enterprise databases, multi-threaded scientific simulations, high-throughput web serving, and CPU-driven machine learning workloads.
